newsitem.title: UK: BT seen mulling MCI merger at board meeting.
newsitem.headline: BT seen mulling MCI merger at board meeting.

text.p: British Telecommunications directors will probably discuss the terms of its troubled $20 billion merger with America's MCI Communications Corp when they meet to approve first-quarter results this week, analysts said.

BT said on Tuesday it welcomed news that America's top telephone regulator looked set to back the merger, but declined to comment on the progress of its review into the U.S. carrier after MCI's profit warning three weeks ago.

Analysts have said Monday's endorsement of the merger by Reed Hundt, the chairman of the Federal Communications Commission, may be timed to give Washington-based MCI a boost as BT's board meets ahead of results on Thursday.
The FCC is the final regulatory body to look at the largest trans-Atlantic merger on record and Hundt urged his agency to swiftly approve a deal he said was in the public interest.
A BT spokesman said only that the company was pleased with the statement.

BT, which has promised to take steps to ensure competition is upheld on the U.S.-British telephone route, has been consistently confident of winning regulatory blessing for its plans to buy the 80 percent of the long-distance carrier it does not already own.

But some analysts warn that the FCC's idea of what is in the public interest might not apply to BT investors as MCI uses BT's financial muscle to help step up investments to break into lucrative, but unyielding, local U.S. markets.

"The U.S. public interest is -- of course -- that BT invest their strong UK cashflows into the U.S. local market to break the Baby Bells' (local operators') monopoly," noted Oliver Ehrenberg, telecoms analyst at Robert Fleming.
Few analysts believe BT will abandon the deal, although terms might be re-adjusted after MCI's forecasts of substantially higher-than-expected losses.

But institutional investors are growing increasingly impatient at what they call a news blackout from BT since the company launched a thorough review of MCI's businesses and investment plans on July 16.

Ahead of any statement from BT, few brokers are recommending buying BT's shares despite their sharp recent falls. One said he no longer felt the information flow was sufficient to recommend the stock to clients.

"MCI makes sense -- but at what dilution? I'm not sure BT shareholders can stomach a reduction in earnings for two years in a row when there is no real underlying problem with the UK business," says another analyst.
BT's shares have dived from a year high of 504p. They were trading two pence weaker at 419.5p at 1200 GMT.
"The longer BT keep quiet and the longer people are forced to come up with rumours, the worse it can get for them," noted Ehrenberg.

Ehrenberg, who has warned that MCI might prove a financial black hole for BT, expects the British company to make an official announcement soon. "It shouldn't take (finance director) Robert Brace too long...to look through MCI's books and get a feeling what the situation is," he said.
But BT will not be holding a news conference when it reports its first quarter results on Thursday and few analysts expect an official statement on the merger this week.

BT, which expressed surprise and disappointment at MCI's forecasts of up $800 million of losses in its local business this year and more next year, says only that it can rule nothing out ahead of the review's completion.
The company declined to say which of its executives were in the country and which were still at MCI's headquarters in Washington.

"We're not in the business of tracking our executives' moves back and forth across the Atlantic at the moment. Some are there, some are here and yes, they are travelling back and forth from time to time," a spokesman said.
"We announced the review on July 16 and until that review is completed, we have nothing to add."

Analysts expected BT's first quarter pre-tax profits to slip to 830 million pounds ($1.4 billion) to 860 million pounds from 869 million pounds amid increasing competition at home and start-up costs of new operations.
